h1: Choosing a keg washer for a growing brewery
title: Choosing a Keg Washer for a Brewery | Craft Beer School
desc: How to choose a keg washer for a growing brewery: manual, semi-automatic and automatic options, cycle steps, throughput and costs.
teaser: Washing kegs by hand works at 20 kegs a week. At 200 it becomes the job nobody wants and the place infections start.
standfirst: A keg washer is one of the least glamorous purchases a brewery makes. It is also one of the most important for quality, because a dirty keg ruins clean beer. Here is how to pick one that fits your volume.
sections: Why kegs need a proper cycle

A returned keg holds stale beer, yeast and air. Before it is refilled it must be emptied, rinsed, cleaned with hot caustic, rinsed again, sanitised and filled with CO2 so it is under pressure and free of oxygen. Skip a step and you get either infected beer or oxidised beer. Neither is fixable once it reaches the bar.

A typical cycle runs like this:

  1. Purge the remaining beer with air or CO2.
  2. Pre-rinse with water.
  3. Caustic wash, commonly at about 1.5 to 2% and 60 to 80 °C.
  4. Rinse.
  5. Acid rinse or sanitiser such as peracetic acid.
  6. Purge with CO2 and leave the keg under pressure.

• Manual. A keg head connected to a pump and a chemical tank, with valves turned by hand. Cheap, but slow, inconsistent and hard on the person doing it.
  • Semi-automatic. One or two heads with a controller that runs the cycle once you connect the keg and press start. This is where most small breweries begin.
  • Automatic lines. Conveyors, several heads and often filling in the same machine. Only worth it at volumes most Indian craft breweries have not reached yet.

The jump from manual to semi-automatic is usually the one that pays fastest. It removes the human from timing the cycle, which is where shortcuts happen at the end of a long day.

Work out kegs per week now and in two years. Then time the cycle. If one head takes about four minutes per keg including connecting and disconnecting, it washes roughly 15 kegs an hour. A two-head machine running alternately might wash around 25 to 30. Use the supplier's real cycle time, not the brochure's best case.

If you fill 150 kegs a week, a single head needs around ten hours of washing time. That is more than a shift. A second head, or a machine that fills as well as washes, starts to make sense. Our guide on buying kegs covers the keg side of the plan.

• Heated caustic tank with temperature control. Cold caustic does not clean.
  • Recirculating chemicals. Reusing caustic for several cycles saves chemicals and water, as long as you check strength.
  • CO2 purge and pressurisation. Leaving kegs under CO2 keeps oxygen out until filling.
  • Stainless construction. Hot caustic eats cheap fittings.
  • Coupler type. Make sure the washer head fits your keg fittings, whether Sankey S, D or another type.

Keg washing uses a lot of water and sends hot caustic to drain. Plan where that goes. A neutralisation step may be needed before discharge, depending on your local pollution control conditions. In hard water areas, scale builds up in the heater and on the kegs. Treating the rinse water or adding acid rinses regularly keeps both clean.

Check caustic strength with a conductivity meter or a simple titration every day you wash. Strength drops as it picks up beer residue and carbon dioxide. A caustic tank that has quietly fallen to 0.5% is not cleaning anything.

Compare the washer's price, chemicals, power and water against the labour hours it saves. Add the cost of one dumped batch from a dirty keg, which can be the beer, the excise duty already paid and an unhappy outlet. That figure usually settles the argument. Include maintenance too: seals, pumps and heaters wear out. Our contract brewing guide is worth a read if you plan to have someone else fill kegs for you.

Linking equipment choices to output and cost, rather than buying on gut feel, is a skill founders can learn before they need it.

A good washer also helps you track keg condition. Check each keg as it goes on the head: dents, damaged spears, missing caps and worn seals. A keg with a bent spear can leak or fail to clean properly. Pull it out of circulation and repair it rather than refilling it.

Number every keg and record where it goes. Kegs that leave the brewery and do not come back are a quiet but real cost. A keg register, even on a spreadsheet, shows you which outlets hold your kegs longest. In practice it also tells you which outlets to chase for returns before you buy more.

Count last month's keg fills. Time one manual clean from start to finish, honestly. Multiply up to your two-year volume. If the answer is more than half a person's working week, ask three suppliers for a semi-automatic washer quote with a real cycle time written in.
faqs: What temperature should caustic be for keg washing?
Typically around 60 to 80 °C at about 1.5 to 2% strength. Follow your chemical supplier's guidance for the product you use.
Can I wash kegs by hand?
Yes, at low volumes, but it is slow and inconsistent. A semi-automatic washer usually pays for itself once volumes grow beyond a few dozen kegs a week.
Why fill washed kegs with CO2?
CO2 pushes out air so the keg holds no oxygen before filling. Oxygen picked up at filling stales beer quickly, especially hoppy beers.
